name: System1-Agents
summary: Framework that puts System 1 decision models such as Jev, Laya or Cua-S1 in openJiuwen agents to pick one typed option per step; ships browser, desktop-app, game, ALFWorld and ticket-routing agents.
notes: Adjacent because browser and desktop control are two of several shipped domains; the package (s1a) is equally aimed at games, ALFWorld, ticket routing and an injection-guard rail. On a decision turn the System 1 model answers typed choice questions while a chat model keeps planning, typed values and the final answer. The browser front runs a stock openJiuwen browser subagent (pinned ThinkFlowLab fork of agent-core) over @playwright/mcp; its in-page probe numbers the visible controls of the top document's light DOM, and the decision model chooses an element plus an operation head (CLICK, TYPE_TEXT, PRESS_ENTER, SELECT, scrolling). OmniJev instead receives a page screenshot. The desktop agent drives a Windows or macOS app window through the external Cua Driver over MCP, clicking accessibility elements bound to a window snapshot. Decision models are reached through TypeSafe, OpenRouter or served endpoints; Cua-S1 Nano runs in process from a pinned trycua/cua subdirectory. Speed and cost tables in the README are the publisher's single-episode comparisons. The browser files carry Huawei copyright notices with ThinkFlowLab modifications under Apache-2.0.

name: Browser Agent (uiuing)
summary: Chrome side-panel agent whose page engine reads a whole-page semantic DOM snapshot, re-grounds targets by element fingerprints, dispatches DOM events and checks post-conditions before reporting success.
notes: Chrome Manifest V3 extension by uiuing, first released as v0.0.1 (Chrome zip in GitHub releases). The model acts on pages only through the page_act tool, which hands a goal to an engine that builds a semantic snapshot of DOM nodes with roles, accessible names, values, occlusion, open shadow roots and same-origin iframes (packages/extension/src/engine/page/perception.ts), resolves targets by fingerprint against a fresh snapshot and fires click, input, change and key events in the page (engine/page/execute.ts). The page_screenshot tool shows a capture to the user; its description limits the model to other page information rather than the pixels (tools/page.ts). A chrome.debugger channel is used for file uploads and falls back to DOM synthesis. Tools carry read, act or dangerous risk tiers with site allow/block lists and confirmation; verified runs can be saved as skills and replayed over batch rows. Model ports cover OpenAI-compatible, OpenAI Responses and Anthropic APIs. The docs/benchmark.md comparison is publisher-run on the project's own fixtures against its own replica of a viewport-only baseline.

name: OpenBUA
summary: Chrome side-panel agent that works in the user's signed-in browser, reading DOM control inventories and tab screenshots, then clicking, typing and filling forms through injected synthetic events.
notes: Chrome Manifest V3 extension (manifest version 1.9.1) whose agent loop is built on the pi-agent-core and pi-ai packages. Its tools (src/agent/tools.ts) read a paginated inventory of interactive DOM controls including open shadow roots, inspect forms, click elements or screenshot-pixel coordinates (used for canvas editors such as Google Docs), type, scroll, switch and open tabs, upload files, post to social sites and send webmail; capture_tab_screenshot returns the visible-tab image to the model. Actions run as scripts injected with chrome.scripting that dispatch synthetic pointer and mouse events (src/agent/browser-bridge.ts); the manifest requests no debugger permission. Before showing its human CAPTCHA gate, the bridge makes up to two automatic rounds in which a vision model is asked to click inside detected challenge regions (src/agent/captcha-auto.ts). It acts in the user's logged-in sessions and keeps a memory store with optional parallel worker windows. The README ends with 'MIT', but the inspected tree has no license file.

name: ClosePaw
summary: On-device Android agent app that reads the accessibility tree, with optional screenshots, acts through accessibility node actions or gesture taps, and can run on a Shizuku virtual display in the background.
notes: Kotlin app for Android 12 or later with an on-device ReAct loop, subagent delegation, todo and scratchpad tools, markdown memory files and per-app skills. Perception defaults to the accessibility tree; screenshot-only and hybrid modes are options (perception/PerceptionConfig.kt). Clicks try an accessibility ACTION_CLICK on the resolved node and fall back to a dispatched gesture tap (tool/action/ClickExecutor.kt, platform/NodeActionPerformer.kt, platform/AccessibilityGestureInjector.kt). Optional power tools use Shizuku for a background virtual display, Termux for a Linux shell, and Chrome DevTools Protocol scripting of Chrome. A bundled tier list blocks banking, payment, crypto-wallet, password-manager and authenticator packages (assets/security/app_tiers.json), and other apps need per-app approval. Models are reached through OpenAI-compatible endpoints or a ChatGPT/Codex sign-in. The eval/ harness drives AndroidWorld task setup and scoring and launches the app over ADB.

name: Wanta
summary: Electron desktop host for work agents (built-in OpenCode agent plus Claude Code, Codex and Grok adapters) whose bundled integrated browser lets agent and user operate one visible page through ARIA-snapshot refs.
notes: Recorded as adjacent: Wanta is a general agent host whose local tools are files, shell, skills, knowledge and SaaS connectors (OpenConnector), and its only graphical executor is the integrated browser. The Electron main process owns a WebContentsView per task page, Playwright attaches through a custom CDP transport over webContents.debugger, and an authenticated loopback bridge serves seven OpenCode tools: browser_navigate, browser_read (title, URL, dialog state and a Playwright AI-mode ARIA snapshot with refs), browser_click and browser_type on refs or unique selectors, browser_scroll, browser_screenshot and browser_dialog. The user shares the page and completes logins and CAPTCHAs; in Default Access the agent is told to hand sensitive actions to the user, which the design document calls a behavioural policy rather than a system guarantee. External agents keep their own accounts; hosted models, connectors and team workspaces need an OOMOL account. Packages for macOS, Windows and Linux. Root LICENSE is Apache-2.0.

name: OpenJev
summary: Decision models at 1.7B, 4B and 8B that answer typed questions with calibrated probabilities in one pass; trained on browser-agent steps and general decision data, they pick a web agent's next operation and element.
notes: Models and code for an open replacement of a hosted System One decision API. A Qwen3 or Qwen3.5 backbone without its vocabulary head scores each option with a pointer head, so one pass answers every question in a request; a local server exposes POST /v1/systemone. Browser steps arrive as page text, numbered elements and recent actions, and the model chooses an operation (click, type, DONE and others) and a target element. The repository holds the wev package (data conversion for Mind2Web, NNetNav and WebChain, training, calibration, export, serving), teacher-collection scripts, the OpenJev-Bench browser-lane client (2,346 frozen steps stored in the Hub dataset alanhuangya/OpenJev-Data), locked results and the paper source; the paper is a Zenodo deposit (doi 10.5281/zenodo.22941164) with no catalog record. The models also answer general decisions such as triage and routing. Results are publisher-reported, and live-website numbers use an LLM judge.

details.availability: Weights for OpenJev-1.7B, 4B (v0.2) and 8B and the OpenJev-Data dataset are on the Hugging Face Hub; training, evaluation and serving code is on GitHub and PyPI (wev-ai, openjev-ai).
details.training_data_note: Publisher-listed sources: Mind2Web and NNetNav-live browser steps (NNetNav stop labels relabelled by an LLM judge), judge-verified teacher episodes from jev-ultrafast runs on live sites with qwen3-max and later GLM-5.3-Flash as System One, and general typed-decision corpora (Kev decision-v7, typed-decisions, tasksource-jev, jev-distill, typed-decisions-synth). The README warns that some tasksource-jev tasks are research-only and that teacher episodes are model outputs under their provider's terms.

name: OpenComet
summary: Chrome side-panel agent that tags page elements with numbered boxes, redacts faces, credential fields and text PII on-device before a model sees the screenshot and DOM text, and acts through selectors or debugger clicks.
notes: The README presents it as a Smart India Hackathon entry for problem statement 26171, whose listed organisation is ISRO. The Manifest V3 extension (version 1.31.0 at review) is loaded unpacked in Chrome; the README says Firefox has been built from the same source since v1.17.0. src/content/dom-detector.js paints numbered boxes on interactive elements, and the service worker captures the tab through the Chrome debugger or captureVisibleTab, so screenshots carry those marks. In privacy mode, MediaPipe, YOLO, ViT, Tesseract OCR and regex/checksum PII detectors run in the browser, and src/lib/privacy-firewall.js blocks or blanks a frame when sanitizing fails. Actions use selectors, with debugger Input.dispatchMouseEvent clicks where needed, inside a tab-group sandbox with an approval mode. Models: on-device Gemma 4, cloud providers, or Ollama through the bundled server. OpenCometBench is the repository's own test suite; its PII precision/recall uses a synthetic corpus built from the detector's own rules, as the README states, leaving independence outside the measurement.

actions: GUI actions in the rendered workspace (live-UI subset)
content shared or sent through the workspace apps
benchmark_protocol.evaluation: The code release scores each run for utility (required items shared) and contextual-integrity violation (prohibited items leaked), combining deterministic text matching against the scenario's must-share and must-not-share lists with an LLM judge at temperature 0; summaries report utility rate, leak rate and average reward.

counts.population: test_e2e split (subset of test used for live-UI evaluation)

benchmark_protocol.notes: Setting is mixed: the reasoning track scores responses over decoded app states, while the test_e2e subset runs in the rendered web UI. A script recount of the released JSONL files matches every reported split and failure-mode count. The 50 test_e2e IDs all appear in test; seeds share separate IDs.

read_basis: Read the pinned dataset card, Hub API revision record and all three JSONL splits (rows recounted by script), plus the code README, mcts/reward_judge.py and eval/metrics.py at commit 7b3fad42 and the GitHub API records for both linked code repositories. No benchmark was run.

name: UINav: A Practical Approach to Train On-Device Automation Agents
summary: Trains small Android automation agents from demonstrations, using macro actions with status checks, demonstration augmentation, and a referee model that predicts task completion to guide further demonstrations.
notes: The annotation was reviewed against the ACL Anthology landing page and proceedings PDF. Screens are represented from the Android accessibility tree or from pixel-based screen understanding, chosen by heuristics. Evaluation uses the public MoTIF dataset and a demonstration study of 43 tasks across 128 Android apps and websites. This record follows the publisher edition of the work; an arXiv preprint is 2312.10170.

name: Visual Grounding for User Interfaces
summary: Proposes LVG, which detects and grounds the UI element named by a free-form command in an Android screenshot, using layout-guided contrastive learning and synthetic referring expressions generated from Rico screens.
notes: The annotation was reviewed against the ACL Anthology landing page and proceedings PDF. LVG is trained on the UIBert dataset (16,660 referring expressions on 5,682 Android screenshots) plus 22,617 synthetic expressions for 21,282 Rico screens, and the paper reports evaluation on Android data only. The paper names no code release, and no arXiv version was found.

name: OpenWebAgent: An Open Toolkit to Enable Web Agents on Large Language Models
summary: Presents OpenWebAgent, a web automation toolkit that pairs a Chrome plugin with an HTML parser and an action generation module, in a modular framework where developers plug in LLMs or LMMs.
notes: The annotation was reviewed against the ACL Anthology landing page and the proceedings PDF. The PDF exceeds the catalog's 10 MB fetch budget, so only the landing page is a retained receipt. The abstract states that the framework, Chrome plugin and demo video are published in an author GitHub repository.

name: Bardeen
summary: Chrome-extension platform for go-to-market teams whose AI scraper navigates sites, clicks, fills forms and pages through results to collect leads, with an AI template builder and a goal-driven agent mode.
notes: The site footer names Bardeen Inc. as the operator, and the homepage links plans at https://www.bardeen.ai/pricing. The homepage now markets the product for lead sourcing, enrichment with contact data and LLM-based lead qualification, with exports to CSV, Google Sheets, Airtable and Notion; enrichment and qualification concern lead data rather than GUI actions. The scraper page describes an AI builder that navigates a page to produce a scraper template, an agent mode that works through a list of websites toward a stated goal, click and input actions, pagination, background scraping in a separate browser window and running on the user's own machine without shared passwords. The support page calls Bardeen a Chrome extension whose automations can run locally in the browser or in the cloud. The models driving the agents, reliability, pricing terms and the SOC 2, GDPR and CASA claims are publisher statements.

name: WebOlympus: An Open Platform for Web Agents on Live Websites
summary: Presents WebOlympus, an open platform that runs web agents on live websites from a few lines of code or a Chrome extension, with a safety monitor that blocks harmful actions through human or model checks.
notes: The annotation was reviewed against the ACL Anthology landing page and proceedings PDF. The platform observes HTML and screenshots and grounds actions through textual choices, set-of-mark overlays or pixel coordinates. On 50 Mind2Web tasks run on live websites, the paper reports SeeAct success of 48% with textual choices and 56% with set-of-mark grounding. The paper says code will be released for research under an OPEN-RAIL license; no release was checked in this review.

name: WinSpot: GUI Grounding Benchmark with Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Introduces WinSpot, a Windows GUI grounding benchmark of 5,000 manually validated coordinate-instruction pairs, built by having multimodal LLMs label raw desktop screenshots without HTML or accessibility trees.
notes: The annotation was reviewed against the ACL Anthology landing page and proceedings PDF. This short paper is separate from the WinClick preprint arxiv:2503.04730, which also introduces WinSpot and which the paper cites as prior work. Screenshots come from Bing image search over popular Microsoft Store apps, filtered with Phi-3-vision, labeled by an in-house icon detector and aligned with instructions by GPT-4o. The abstract counts 5,000 coordinate-instruction pairs, while the benchmark section describes over 5,000 annotated screenshots from 14 Windows applications.

name: BrowseGPT
summary: Chrome extension with a local Node.js server that lists the visible page's links, buttons and inputs as a numbered outline and asks OpenAI gpt-3.5-turbo for the next CLICK, ENTER_TEXT or NAVIGATE step toward a goal.
notes: Inspected at commit c86c148e (23 July 2024), the latest commit on the default branch. The content script assigns IDs to visible, in-viewport elements and sends the first 100 outline lines with the goal, URL and up to five previous steps to the server, whose few-shot prompt asks gpt-3.5-turbo for one JSON command with a reason; the extension then calls click(), enters text or changes the location. Each submission runs one step, and elements already acted on are left out of later outlines. The Manifest V3 extension is labelled version 2.0. The browsegpt.ai site and its llms.txt describe Claude Haiku 4.5 as the default model with OpenAI GPT as an option; the public repository's server calls only the OpenAI API. The Chrome Web Store build remains uninspected. The repository has no license file, so the code license is unknown. No code was run.

details.availability: Public extension and server source with no license file; the published Chrome Web Store build remains uninspected.

name: AutoBrowser
summary: Chrome side-panel extension that runs a browser-use-style web agent: it indexes a tab's interactive elements and has a user-configured OpenAI-compatible model open tabs, click, type and press keys.
notes: The Chrome Web Store listing names browser-use as its inspiration, shows version 1.1.1 updated February 27, 2025, 38 users and no ratings, and says the developer has not identified as a trader; it links no website or source repository. The inspected version 1.1.1 package has a side panel where the user enters a Base URL, API key and model ID for an OpenAI-compatible chat API. The agent numbers the page's interactive DOM elements and calls four actions (open a new tab, click an element by index, type into an element by index, press a key), which bundled Puppeteer executes through the chrome.debugger protocol. No image input to the model was found in the package. The awesome-web-agents list describes the extension as using Claude Computer Use; the inspected version leaves that claim unsupported.

details.availability: Chrome Web Store extension; no source repository is published

name: Browserable
summary: Self-hosted browser-agent platform with a JS SDK and REST API: a planner sets high-level steps, and a runner reads a screenshot and a numbered DOM chunk to pick Playwright actions in a local or hosted browser.
notes: Inspected at commit a3af19a6 (27 August 2025). The README sets up a Docker Compose stack (UI server, tasks server, MongoDB, Redis and MinIO) in which the user supplies one LLM key (Gemini, OpenAI or Claude) and a Steel or Hyperbrowser key; tasks/services/browser.js also accepts Browserbase or the repository's own browser service, which launches Playwright Chromium. In tasks/agents/browserable.js the act-on-tab action calls simpleActionHelper, whose loop takes a plain page screenshot and the current chunk of DOM elements with XPaths, asks a planner for high-level steps (replanning after five steps), and asks a runner for a Playwright method, arguments and element number; the older DOM-only and vision act helpers are commented out at that call site. The repository also contains deep-research and generative agents. The README's 90.4% WebVoyager figure is publisher-reported. The README names Stagehand among the open-source projects it builds on. No code was run.

details.availability: Public source for the self-hosted services, browser service and JS SDK; no hosted service was tested.
details.license_components_note: ui/LICENSE carries a separate MIT notice, copyright 2015 Gil Barbara; the root browserable notice is distinct.

name: Dex
summary: ThirdLayer's Chrome extension that keeps an operational memory of a user's work tools and runs agents that navigate tabs and fill forms in the browser, alongside Gmail, Slack and CRM integrations.
notes: The homepage footer names ThirdLayer, Inc. as the operator. getdexterity.com, the address in the discovery source, answers with a 301 redirect to www.joindex.com, and a February 2025 Wayback Machine capture of getdexterity.com, titled Dexterity AI, describes the same Dex browser product with natural-language navigation, cross-tab automation and form filling. The current homepage presents browser control (navigating tabs, filling forms) as one of four capabilities beside an operational graph, an editable knowledge manual and event- or schedule-triggered agents that work through integrations with Gmail, Slack, CRMs and other tools. The prompts in its use-case library mostly name connected apps such as HubSpot, Gmail, Slack and Notion; the scope is adjacent to browser actions. The pricing page lists the browser extension among the features of its paid individual plans, and the homepage marks a desktop app as coming soon. The models behind the agents, reliability and the security and privacy claims are publisher statements.

name: Are CAPTCHAs Still Bot-hard? Generalized Visual CAPTCHA Solving with Agentic Vision Language Model
summary: Presents Halligan, a VLM agent that abstracts visual CAPTCHAs into frames, elements and keypoints and solves each as a search problem through generated interaction code, tested on 2,600 challenges of 26 types.
notes: Reviewed against the USENIX Security 2025 proceedings PDF and the authors' project page halligan.pages.dev, which the paper names as its website. In the benchmark comparison Halligan used GPT-4o and acted through PyAutoGUI on CAPTCHAs replayed from a local Flask server. The paper reports 1,577 of 2,600 benchmark challenges solved (60.7%) and a 70.6% average solve rate on previously unseen CAPTCHAs over a 30-day field study run through human-driven CAPTCHA farms. It names Zenodo record 10.5281/zenodo.15580923 for its source code and benchmark. No arXiv version was found.
read_basis: Read the full proceedings PDF text (abstract, threat model, approach, benchmark, experiment setup, ethics and open-science sections) and the project page.

name: Ace
summary: General Agents' desktop autopilot, trained on recorded expert behavior, that predicts clicks, keystrokes and other actions from screenshots; its API client ships a macOS controller that executes them.
notes: The Ace page describes a computer autopilot that uses the mouse and keyboard on the user's desktop, says it was trained by software specialists and domain experts on over a million tasks, and charts publisher figures for click-prediction accuracy for ace-control-medium and ace-control-small against Operator, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, UI-TARS-72B-SFT and other models, plus action latency. The About page says Ace learns from experts' screen recordings with mouse and keyboard logs, and that General Agents is developing video-language-action models. The official Python client (generalagents-python 0.1.1 at commit d36f6a8) posts a WebP screenshot, the instruction and recent actions to /v1/control/predict on api.generalagents.com; its macOS Computer class captures the screen with screencapture and performs clicks, drags, scrolls, key presses and typing through pyautogui. Apache-2.0 covers the client's code. At review time api.generalagents.com and docs.generalagents.com had DNS resolution failures; the reviewed pages leave pricing, download and sign-up paths unspecified, so current availability remains unknown.

details.availability: Hosted models reached through an API; the API and documentation hosts had DNS resolution failures at review time, and pricing and sign-up paths remain unpublished.

name: Claude Code
summary: Anthropic agentic coding tool for terminal, IDE, desktop and web, with an opt-in computer-use preview that screenshots and operates approved apps on macOS (CLI) and on macOS and Windows (Desktop).
notes: A general coding agent, so the scope is adjacent. GUI control is an opt-in research preview for Pro and Max plans, provided in the CLI by a built-in computer-use MCP server on macOS and in the Desktop app on macOS and Windows. Claude Code tries MCP servers, Bash and the Claude in Chrome integration first and reserves screen control for remaining apps. Browser automation runs through the separately cataloged Claude for Chrome extension (url:07b6bbce7ce26a847f79). The docs.anthropic.com address redirects to code.claude.com/docs.

name: HARPA AI
summary: Chrome extension that brings chat models to any web page for summaries and writing, with an automation engine whose user-built commands navigate, click, paste, extract and monitor pages around AI steps.
notes: Recorded as adjacent: the publisher's getting-started guide presents HARPA mainly as a page-aware AI chat for summarizing, writing and search, with an AUTOMATE tab for page monitors and scheduled commands. The reviewed guides describe page actions as user-built command steps (NAVIGATE, CLICK, PASTE, SCROLL, EXTRACT, RUN JS) that run in the open tab and can be combined with GPT steps. The homepage's email-obfuscation markup changes on every request.

name: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
summary: AWS managed agent platform whose Browser tool runs isolated cloud browser sessions with automation and live-view streams and optional recording, alongside runtime, memory, gateway and code-execution services.
notes: A general agent hosting platform, so the scope is adjacent. Its computer-interaction component is AgentCore Browser: a containerized browser reached through a WebSocket automation endpoint (usable from Strands, Nova Act or Playwright) and a live-view endpoint where a person can watch the session and interact with it directly. Sessions default to 15 minutes and last at most 8 hours. Session recording, available for custom browsers, stores DOM changes, user actions, console logs and network events in the customer's S3 bucket. Amazon Nova Act (url:dec156cbf0cb1181f7b6) is cataloged separately. The landing URL redirects to its trailing-slash form over plain HTTP, so evidence is read from the HTTPS trailing-slash address.

name: Wuying Agentic Mobile
summary: Alibaba Cloud Wuying service that runs Qwen-driven agents (MobileUseAgent with OpenClaw) in cloud Android containers to carry out natural-language tasks across apps, for process automation and app testing.
notes: The overview describes MobileUseAgent, an Android agent built for Wuying Cloud Phone that parses the native Android control tree, joined to the OpenClaw agent framework, with Qwen models for screen perception and instruction understanding; it also lists social-app engagement that imitates human behavior to avoid platform risk controls as a use case. The quick-start page, reached from the discovered URL whose cloud-phone-mobileclaw slug now redirects to cloud-phone-jvs-mobile, calls the service a public beta sold as monthly node plans with credits for model use, and sends tasks to the OpenClaw agent from a chat page. The X-PLUG/MobileAgent README announces Mobile-Agent-v3.5 on Wuying Cloud Phone and links that page; the linked Alibaba Cloud pages leave the Mobile-Agent-v3.5 name unstated. Receipts use the Markdown exports of the help pages because their HTML embeds a per-request tracking ID.

name: Tongyi UI Agent API
summary: Alibaba Cloud Model Studio API that returns the next GUI action with its reasoning for a screenshot and task, with a mobile pipeline and a PC pipeline using planner, worker, reflector and memory agents.
notes: The page (version V0.0.1) documents a DashScope endpoint for the gui-owl app that takes a screenshot URL, a task instruction, a session ID and optional operation hints (add_info), and returns the next action, such as a click or swipe with screen coordinates, with a thought and an explanation. Requests set device_type to mobile or pc and use the model pre-gui_owl_7b; the PC pipeline also names worker, manager, reflector and notetaker models and can enable the reflection and memory agents. The page states that the agent targets phones, in-car systems, TVs and PCs, names no mobile operating system, and lists usage as free for a limited time. The X-PLUG/MobileAgent README links this page as a limited-time free Mobile-Agent-v3 API; the page itself names no paper or released checkpoint, so no relation to the Mobile-Agent or GUI-Owl records is asserted. The receipt uses the Markdown export because the HTML embeds a per-request tracking ID.

name: AdapAction: Adaptive Target Action Backdoor Attack against GUI Agents
summary: Backdoor attack that fine-tunes GUI agents on teacher-written malicious trajectories, so a trigger makes the agent choose a harmful action fitting the current screen and instruction; tested on AitZ and AndroidControl.
notes: The annotation was reviewed against the CVF open-access landing page and PDF. A teacher model (for example Gemini 2.5 Pro) writes malicious reasoning trajectories drawn from a five-category malicious action library, and the agent learns them by supervised fine-tuning, which the paper calls Context-Aware Behavioral Imitation. Main results fine-tune Qwen2-VL-2B and Qwen2-VL-7B at a 0.1 poisoning ratio with a blended visual trigger; an AndroidWorld emulator deployment through Mobile-Agent-v3 is described in the supplementary material. The paper links no code release or arXiv version.

name: RealWeb: A Benchmark for Universal Instruction Following in Realistic Web Services Navigation
summary: Introduces RealWeb, a Chinese benchmark of 11,739 instructions on 40 real websites with annotated screenshots and slot trees, plus a baseline that detects page regions, parses instructions and acts on the pages.
notes: The annotation was reviewed against the IEEE Xplore abstract page, the Crossref-deposited citation and the authors' Gitee repository README. The abstract counts 110 pages and names the baseline WeServe, reporting a 68.61% success rate; the README counts 119 pages across 15 domains. At the inspected commit the repository's Codes folder holds only a placeholder file, while the dataset files are present. No arXiv version was found.
read_basis: Read the IEEE Xplore abstract page (title, abstract, authors, DOI, pages 342-351, ICWS 2024), the Crossref BibTeX deposit, the Crossref works record, and the Gitee README and recursive tree at commit 55266af1. The IEEE page bytes change on every request, so the stable Crossref citation is the retained primary receipt. No data download or result reproduction.

name: LongHorizonUI: A Unified Framework for Robust long-horizon Task Automation of GUI Agent
summary: Training-free GUI agent that indexes screen elements via icon detection and OCR, checks each step with multi-level reflection and recovers by fallback clicks or rollback; introduces LongGUIBench, tasks over 15 steps.
notes: Reviewed against the ICLR 2026 proceedings page and PDF; the OpenReview forum lists it as an ICLR 2026 Poster. LongHorizonUI's components run without fine-tuning, with Gemini 2.5 Pro as the default backbone; Appendix D.6 also reports Gemini 1.5 Flash and Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbones. LongGUIBench tasks need more than 15 steps across games and general apps; the paper states 371 scenarios but gives 207 game scenarios in Section 2.1 and 224 in Appendix D.2, leaving the benchmark's device platform unnamed. Other reported evaluations are ScreenSpot grounding, AndroidControl and GUI-Odyssey, plus zero-shot AndroidWorld and OSWorld runs in Appendix D.5. The paper points to kane2kang.github.io/LongHorizonUI for code. No arXiv version was found.
read_basis: Read the ICLR proceedings page metadata and abstract, and the full proceedings PDF text (method, LongGUIBench construction, implementation details, benchmark appendix and zero-shot transfer appendix); checked the OpenReview note in a browser. No code execution or result reproduction.

name: Computer Agent Arena: Toward Human-Centric Evaluation and Analysis of Computer-Use Agents
summary: Crowdsourced arena where users set tasks on cloud Ubuntu or Windows desktops, watch two anonymous computer-use agents attempt them side by side and vote; reports 2,201 votes over 12 agents.
notes: Reviewed against the ICLR 2026 proceedings page and abstract, the full proceedings PDF and the platform README at commit 4536036; the OpenReview forum lists it as an ICLR 2026 Poster. Two anonymized agents run the same user-written instruction in parallel, identically initialized Ubuntu or Windows virtual machines on AWS EC2, shown to users through a browser VNC view and synchronized replays; the paper turns the pairwise votes into a Bradley-Terry ranking and also collects optional step-level labels. It reports 2,201 filtered votes from 1,058 users over 12 agents, compares pure GUI agents with agents that also call tools or write code, and links github.com/xlang-ai/computer-agent-arena for the platform and a Hugging Face page for the collected data; neither release was reviewed here. No arXiv version was found.
read_basis: Read the ICLR proceedings page metadata and abstract, the full proceedings PDF text (system design, agent implementation, ranking method, data statistics and appendices), and the platform README at commit 4536036; checked the OpenReview note in a browser. The 18.8 MB PDF exceeds the catalog fetch budget, so it is not a retained receipt. No code execution or result reproduction.

name: Learning to Contextualize Web Pages for Enhanced Decision Making by LLM Agents
summary: Trains a separate language model to rewrite lengthy web page observations into focused descriptions for LLM web agents, keeping training targets that let several LLMs predict the correct next action.
notes: Reviewed against the ICLR 2025 proceedings page and PDF; the OpenReview forum lists it as an ICLR 2025 Poster. LCoW's contextualization module reads the task, previous actions and a raw page observation such as an accessibility tree, and is retrained each iteration by supervised fine-tuning on the sampled rewrites that let several LLM agents recover the ground-truth action in successful trajectories. Appendix B fine-tunes Phi-3-mini-Instruct for WebShop and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for WorkArena and WebArena. WebShop and WorkArena are the main benchmarks; a 165-task WebArena subset tests generalization to unseen task types. The same paper is posted on arXiv as 2503.10689 with the comment "Accepted to ICLR 2025". The paper points to lcowiclr2025.github.io for code.
read_basis: Read the ICLR proceedings page metadata and abstract and the full proceedings PDF text (method, training algorithm, benchmark setup, results and Appendix B implementation details); checked the OpenReview note in a browser and the arXiv 2503.10689 abstract page. No code execution or result reproduction.

name: Grounding Multimodal Large Language Model in GUI World
summary: Trains a 0.4B SAM-initialized GUI grounding model on 0.5M auto-collected web screenshots with 35M element annotations, then links it to a Qwen-VL planner through a position token for MiniWob, AITW and Mind2Web.
verify_terms: Grounding Multimodal Large Language Model in GUI World
notes: Reviewed against the ICLR 2025 proceedings page and PDF; the OpenReview forum lists it as an ICLR 2025 Poster. The grounding model, AssistGUIGrounder (AGG), pairs a SAM-pretrained ViT image encoder and a transformer query encoder with a two-layer box decoder. The data engine loads Common Crawl pages from 118 domains in a browser such as Chrome, scrolls them with Page Down and reads element data through UI Automation; grounding training used 0.36M web images with 22M annotations after smoothing, plus 27K mobile screenshots from WidgetCaption and RICO. ScreenSpot grounding covers mobile, desktop and web screenshots; agent fine-tuning covers MiniWob, AITW and Mind2Web. The paper gives github.com/showlab/AssistGUIGround for code and data; that repository returned HTTP 404 on 2026-10-19. No arXiv version was found.
read_basis: Read the ICLR proceedings page metadata and abstract, and the full proceedings PDF text (data engine, model architecture, agent integration, experimental setup, result tables and data appendix); checked the OpenReview note through the api2 notes endpoint in a browser. No code execution or result reproduction.

name: AutomotiveUI-Bench-4K
summary: Offline test set of 998 photos and screenshots of in-vehicle infotainment screens from 15 brands, with 4,208 English annotations for locating UI elements and judging expected results as passed or failed.
notes: Sparks Solutions publishes one ungated test split of 22 Parquet shards at revision d760810c. The card describes mostly photographs of in-vehicle infotainment displays plus some direct screenshots such as Android Auto; its per-brand image counts cover 13 car brands, Apple CarPlay and Google Android Auto and sum to 998. No catalog platform facet fits infotainment systems, so the environment is unspecified. Each annotation pairs a bounding box with either an imperative test action or an expected-result statement labeled passed or failed; UI text is German or English and annotations are English. The card's example code runs the publisher's ELAM-7B model, and its results table is publisher-reported. The card cites arXiv 2505.05895 (Ernhofer et al., 2025). CC-BY-4.0 is the card's data declaration.

details.availability: Ungated test split of 22 Parquet shards on the Hub; the card includes example inference and scoring code.

focus: grounding infotainment UI elements from test-action commands
judging expected-result statements as passed or failed
observations: photographs and screenshots of in-vehicle infotainment displays
actions: point or bounding box for the referenced UI element
passed or failed verdict for expected results
benchmark_protocol.evaluation: The card's scoring script counts a grounding hit when the predicted point, or the center of a predicted box, lies inside the annotated box, and scores expected-result verdicts against the passed or failed labels, overall and by UI language.

counts.population: test split, the only split, at revision d760810c
Test Action rows in the test split, from the Hub dataset viewer's column statistics
Expected Result rows in the test split (1,375 passed, 564 failed), from the Hub dataset viewer's column statistics

benchmark_protocol.notes: Image and annotation totals are the card's. The class split comes from the Hub dataset viewer's statistics for the test split, whose 4,208 rows match the card; the language column is the UI language (2,220 German and 1,988 English rows).

name: In-Context Teacher–Student Guidance for Open-Weight Browser Agents
summary: Training-free protocol that turns a teacher model's offline reasoning traces into prompt guidance for open-weight browser agents; on MiniWoB++ it lifts solved student-task pairs from 208 to 271 across ten students.
notes: The annotation was reviewed against the publisher PDF and the Crossref deposit for its DOI. The method, In-Context Learning Guidance (ICLG), has GPT-5.1 solve tasks offline and appends its reasoning fields alone to the student prompt; the teacher's low-level actions stay outside that prompt, and teacher calls precede the student run. Evaluation serves the 130 MiniWoB++ tasks locally, caps each run at 5 minutes and 25 interaction steps, counts a score of at least 0.5 as solved, and reports single runs: seven of ten students improve and three lose one task. Retry and refined-prompt ablations cover three students. The paper names no code release or arXiv version.

name: Starizon AI
summary: Chrome side-panel agent that researches across tabs, bookmarks and a local knowledge base, and hands click-and-type tasks on signed-in sites to its Agent S6 browser agent, with replays, schedules and page monitors.
notes: The terms of service name Starizon Ltd as the provider of the website, browser extension and related services. Agent S6 navigates, clicks, types and fills in forms in the browser session the user is already signed in to; it stops for confirmations, sign-ins, choices between options and blocked pages, and waits for the user before irreversible actions such as submitting or paying. Chat history, the Knowledge Base and Spaces are stored in the browser profile, while prompts and task context, including page screenshots when browser actions need them, go to the chosen model service or to the user's own API key. The about page claims over 70% on Online-Mind2Web with visual understanding and DOM preprocessing; that score, reliability and pricing terms are publisher statements.

name: Gym-Anything
summary: Runtime and CUA-World task suite that turn real applications on Ubuntu, Windows 11, Android and macOS into screen-observing, mouse-and-keyboard agent environments with setup scripts and program verifiers.
notes: Official code of the Gym-Anything paper. The README describes three parts that can be used separately: the core runtime (src/gym_anything), the CUA-World benchmark (benchmarks/cua_world) and reference agents for Claude, Gemini, Qwen, Kimi and other models. The inspected environment configs (Moodle, Power BI Desktop, an Android AVD calculator and macOS Finder) declare screen observations with mouse and keyboard actions on Ubuntu GNOME, Windows 11, Android AVD 34 and macOS bases; the Finder config also exposes a UI tree, and macOS environments sit in a separate benchmarks/cua_world-macos suite. A task such as moodle_env/enroll_student pairs setup and export hooks with a verifier.py program check and a VLM checklist file. extras/research/software_as_env/creation_audit implements the paper's environment creation-and-audit pipeline, driven by Claude Code by default or Codex CLI. Runners (Docker, Apptainer, QEMU, AVD, AVF, Modal, local and Sandweave) differ in caching, snapshot and recording support. Code was read.

details.availability: Public runtime, CUA-World environment and task definitions with verifiers and split manifests, reference agents and the environment creation-and-audit pipeline.

focus: long-horizon computer use in professional and enterprise software
conversion of arbitrary applications into agent environments
benchmark_protocol.evaluation: Each task's task.json names a program check (verifier.py) that runs after the episode, with pre-task setup and post-task export hooks; task folders also carry a VLM checklist file.

counts.population: applications processed into CUA-World (paper v1 abstract)

benchmark_protocol.notes: The paper's application and task totals and the repository's verified manifest are different populations; these counts are reported separately. Per-environment split files list train and test tasks, and several cover variant folders of one application; these counts are reported separately.

name: Proxy Lite
summary: Convergence AI's open-weights web agent runner: a Playwright Chromium loop that sends annotated screenshots and numbered element lists to proxy-lite-3b and executes its click, type, scroll and navigation tool calls.
notes: The repository is the scaffold for Convergence AI's proxy-lite-3b model: a CLI (proxy), a Streamlit app and a Runner that loops a solver and a webbrowser environment. By default it calls a demo endpoint on Hugging Face Spaces, which the README reserves for demonstrations; it recommends serving convergence-ai/proxy-lite-3b with vLLM and the hermes tool-call parser for production. The webbrowser environment (src/proxy_lite/environments/webbrowser.py) launches Chromium through Playwright with playwright_stealth, injects JavaScript to find interactable elements, and by default sends a screenshot annotated with numbered bounding boxes plus a text list of the marked elements; earlier screenshots are dropped from the context. BrowserTool exposes goto, google_search, click, type, scroll, back, wait, reload and do_nothing actions addressed by mark_id. The README says the model is meant to complete tasks autonomously and may struggle with logins or user-confirmed steps. Model weights are not in this repository. Code was read.

details.availability: Public agent scaffold, CLI and Streamlit app; the proxy-lite-3b weights are published separately on Hugging Face.

value.basis: The repository LICENSE file states that the work is licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0 (a notice, not the legal code); recorded for code only; it is not applied to the proxy-lite-3b weights or the hosted Proxy service.

code.reason: The repository LICENSE file states that the work is licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0 (a notice, not the legal code); recorded for code only; it is not applied to the proxy-lite-3b weights or the hosted Proxy service.

name: MirrorGuard code
summary: MirrorGuard pipeline that synthesizes risky and benign computer-use trajectories in a text-based GUI simulator, builds unsafe-to-safe thought corrections for training, and plugs the corrector into OSWorld-style agents.
notes: Official WhitzardAgent code for the MirrorGuard paper. The VM documentation says the default VM runs Ubuntu 24.04 with 4 CPUs and 8 GiB RAM, that `beam vm new` adds a desktop to fresh images, and that VMs are CPU-only. The desktop documentation covers screenshots, display resizing, mouse moves, clicks, X11 key presses, pasted text, scrolling, dragging, launching GUI programs and recording the guest screen from Python, JavaScript and the CLI; the desktop browser is Chrome on x86-64 and Firefox on ARM64. The homepage footer links the beam-cloud/beta9 repository (serverless GPU inference, sandboxes and background jobs, AGPL-3.0 per the GitHub API); whether it contains the VM desktop was not checked.

name: Gumloop
summary: Business agent platform whose agents work through app connectors and can turn on a Chromium browser that clicks, types, signs in with saved logins and hands control to a person when a site needs it.
notes: Recorded as adjacent: Gumloop presents itself as a platform for building, sharing and running AI agents for business teams, which work mainly through app connectors, MCP servers and APIs, and its help pages advise using the agent browser only when no connector or API covers a task. The agent browser is an ability turned on per custom agent, and on Enterprise organizations it is off by default until an admin adds it to a role. It runs Chromium on the agent's computer, which shares the agent's code sandbox, and opens pages, clicks, types, scrolls and switches tabs. Gumloop types saved logins and 2FA codes for the agent without showing them to the model, keeps sign-ins in browser profiles, offers residential proxies and desktop or Pixel 7 mobile emulation, and pauses to hand the live browser to a person at logins, CAPTCHAs or purchase confirmations. Every browser step is recorded for replay. Agents can also be reached from Slack, Microsoft Teams, email and text messages.

name: HyperWrite Personal Assistant
summary: Browser agent from HyperWrite that carries out typed requests such as searching, making reservations and filling out forms by operating the user's Chrome browser through the HyperWrite extension.
notes: The site footer names OthersideAI as the publisher of HyperWrite, which its llms.txt describes mainly as an AI writing and productivity assistant with a document editor, TypeAhead sentence prediction in a Chrome extension, Personas and a library of AI tools. The Personal Assistant page presents HyperWrite's AI agent as able to use the browser to complete tasks, with examples such as organizing a Gmail inbox, booking a flight, ordering a pizza and finding candidates on LinkedIn. The AI Agent tool page says the agent executes tasks in the user's browser through the HyperWrite extension, searching, navigating websites, filling out forms and interacting with web applications, and lists a limited free trial with paid Premium and Ultra plans. The Personal Assistant page also carries writing and research copy and leftover placeholder text, and its FAQ describes only the extension's writing features. The agent's model, current availability and reliability remain unverified in the reviewed evidence.

name: Komos
summary: Hosted automation platform whose task flows use a prompt-driven agent to navigate, click, type and extract on websites in a cloud Chromium sandbox or self-hosted runner, built from narrated screen recordings or chat.
notes: The documentation describes a task as a reusable automation graph. Its Agent Action node handles browser steps (navigating, clicking, filling forms, scrolling, extracting) from a natural-language prompt, can also call integrations and inspect captured network requests, and accepts screenshots as visual references. A task can be trained from a narrated screen or tab recording of up to five minutes, which Komos turns into a plan, or built step by step in a visual builder. Runs use a fresh or persistent cloud Chromium sandbox on Daytona compute, or a self-hosted runner on a Windows or macOS host that can reuse SSO sessions; the Chrome extension path is retired. The built-in assistant Moss creates, schedules and debugs tasks from chat and is also reachable from coding agents through an MCP server. The agent's model is unspecified.

name: Browse AI
summary: No-code web scraping and monitoring platform whose robots replay recorded clicks, typed inputs, dropdown choices, logins and pagination on target sites, or let AI build the table, then extract data on a schedule.
notes: The help center describes two ways to train a robot: Table Studio, where AI builds the data table from a URL, and Robot Studio, where the user shows the robot what to capture through visual point-and-click training; the llms.txt file also lists a Chrome extension for robot training. Trained robots mimic a user to sign in with stored credentials, fill forms and searches, click buttons, toggles and dropdowns, paginate and scroll, capture screenshots and run on schedules or in bulk, and the llms.txt file states cloud-based execution. The interactions serve data extraction and change monitoring. Prices, usage figures and reliability are publisher statements.

name: Cekura
summary: Service whose browser agent navigates a customer's SaaS product to check whether its documentation is still accurate, then reports what to fix with summaries, session replays and LLM and browser action traces.
notes: Customers send their documentation as it is together with an account for the product, and the agent checks the materials against the live product. The page's FAQ, rendered from its script bundle, calls Cekura an AI web agent that keeps SaaS product documentation up to date for knowledge and customer success teams, says the team sets up the service personally, and says model providers retain no data. The page publishes no self-serve signup, pricing or technical documentation; contact is by email or a booked call. A separate site, cekura.ai, presents a Cekura product for testing voice and chat AI agents; the relationship to cekura.io remains unspecified. Nothing was run.

name: CloudCruise
summary: Managed browser-automation platform for healthcare portals and EHRs in which a builder agent turns a chat description into a reusable workflow graph that runs in cloud VMs and a maintenance agent repairs.
notes: The homepage targets payer-portal and EHR workflows and says every run executes in a VM with laptop-like fingerprints and human-like input, with queued concurrency, video replay, per-action screenshots and logs, and HIPAA-compliant infrastructure. The documentation says the builder agent opens a live browser preview, navigates the target site, asks clarifying questions and turns confirmed actions into a node-and-edge graph that later runs deterministically, with model calls confined to building the graph. Click nodes target elements either by XPath or through an LLM vision mode labelled AI (Screenshot). The maintenance agent classifies failures from the error screenshot, page state and selector signals, then recovers in place, asks for input, retries or hands the workflow to the builder agent. Citrix virtual desktops are automated through their HTML5 browser client using the screenshot mode. Runs start through an API with TypeScript and Python SDKs.

name: dassi
summary: Side-panel extension for Chrome, Edge and Brave whose agent reads pages, takes screenshots, clicks, types, fills forms and manages tabs in the user's signed-in browser, with saved skills, schedules and a choice of model.
notes: Omnify Labs of San Francisco builds dassi. The documentation says the agent identifies elements by role, text and position, can run JavaScript in the page, uses screenshots to verify its work and to handle coordinate-based interfaces, and asks the user to approve a plan before visiting new domains or acting on sensitive pages; passwords, payment details and CAPTCHA solving are outside its stated actions. The homepage describes teaching a job once, scheduled runs in the user's open browser, an editable memory of corrections and per-site JavaScript helpers the agent writes for itself, while the documentation's limitations page still says it does not run tasks in the background or on a schedule. Models include Claude, GPT, Gemini and local models, through managed credits or the user's own key. The documentation source, omnify-labs/dassi-docs, is CC-BY-4.0 per the GitHub API; the license applies to documentation alone.

name: Dia
summary: AI browser from The Browser Company for macOS and Windows whose assistant reads open tabs and connected work apps, with an approval-gated agentic mode that fills forms and drafts replies on the current site.
notes: The homepage presents Dia as a work browser: a morning brief, reports and slide decks assembled from tabs and connected tools such as Slack, Notion, Teams and GSuite, plus profiles, split views and tab grouping. The security page describes the agent's safeguards: each chat starts with access limited to its current tab and read actions until the user grants more, form fills and email drafts are shown for approval before insertion, irreversible actions stay as drafts, agentic mode sees approved context and stays on the approved website, and password fields and irreversible action buttons are hidden from it. The same page names GPT, Claude and Gemini as the underlying models and says The Browser Company is part of Atlassian.

name: Strawberry
summary: Agentic desktop browser for macOS and Windows whose AI companions open sites, click through flows and work inside the user's signed-in accounts, asking for approval before sending, paying or deleting.
notes: Dendrite Systems, a team based in Stockholm, publishes Strawberry. Its llms.txt describes companions as persistent assistants that are briefed once and remember across sessions, routines that run work on a schedule, saved skills that re-run a workflow, and 93 native integrations with 1,254 operations alongside work done in the browser session the user is signed into; companions ask for approval before sending email, making payments or taking destructive actions. The browser-agent page says a companion plans the work, opens the sites, moves between tabs, clicks through flows and uses an app integration when that is faster than browsing. Regular browsing is free, while companion work draws on monthly credits, with a free plan of 500 credits and paid tiers. The llms.txt also says the publisher retracted its February 2026 comparison benchmark after an audit and now publishes a measurement standard for results.

name: Webfuse
summary: Web augmentation proxy that serves a site inside the user's browser and lets AI agents read DOM, screenshot or accessibility-tree snapshots and click, type or scroll through an automation API and a session MCP server.
notes: Webfuse serves an existing website through a configurable proxy session and injects Extensions on the client side without changes to the site's code. Its Automation API, callable from an Extension, provides perception (DOM snapshot, Base64 screenshot of the page, accessibility tree, text selection) and actuation (click, type, scroll, select, key press, mouse move, text selection), targeting an element, CSS selector, point coordinate or Webfuse element ID across shadow DOM and iframes; the screenshot method is documented for Chromium-based browsers only. The Session MCP Server exposes the same tools, plus navigate and page info, to MCP clients authenticated with a Space automation key. tool.applyD2Snap() applies the DOM downsampling method of arXiv 2508.04412, whose second author, Nicholas Piël, is named on the about page as Webfuse's CEO and founder; the about page also says Webfuse grew out of the team's Surfly session technology. The pricing page lists Spark and Forge monthly plans metered in virtual minutes, a custom Foundry tier and a 14-day free trial.

name: UI-Hawk: Unleashing the Screen Stream Understanding for Mobile GUI Agents
summary: Mobile GUI agent whose history-aware visual encoder reads earlier screenshots with the current one, trained by a curriculum from grounding, referring, screen QA and summarization to navigation; adds the FunUI benchmark.
notes: Reviewed against the EMNLP 2025 proceedings page and the full proceedings PDF. The PDF (10.9 MB) exceeds the receipt size limit, so the retained receipt is the landing page with its complete abstract. Per the PDF, UI-Hawk replaces TextHawk's language model with Qwen2-7B and encodes each history screenshot at a quarter of its size in 144 visual tokens; FunUI holds 2,150 Chinese and 9,347 English Android screens, and navigation is evaluated on GUI-Odyssey+ (GUIOdyssey clicks re-annotated with element boxes) and the authors' Chinese GUI-Zouwu episodes. An earlier version titled 'UI-Hawk: Unleashing the Screen Stream Understanding for GUI Agents' was posted on Preprints.org on 30 August 2024 (DOI 10.20944/preprints202408.2137.v1) by the same six authors. The paper points to github.com/IMNearth/UIHawk for code and data.
read_basis: Read the ACL Anthology landing page metadata and abstract, the full proceedings PDF text (method, data collection, FunUI and navigation sections), the Preprints.org page through its 2026-03-14 Wayback capture, and the Crossref records for both DOIs. No code execution or result reproduction.

name: A Survey on Benchmarks of LLM-based GUI Agents
summary: Surveys LLM-based GUI agent benchmarks in three task tiers (grounding and QA, multi-step navigation, open-world environments), comparing their datasets, environments and metrics, and outlines open evaluation gaps.
verify_terms: A Survey on Benchmarks of LLM-based GUI Agents
notes: A TechRxiv preprint (version 1, 16 December 2025) that has not been peer reviewed. The full text tabulates grounding and QA benchmarks such as ScreenQA, ScreenSpot-Pro and OSWorld-G, navigation benchmarks such as VisualWebArena, AndroidControl and GUI-Odyssey, and open-world benchmarks such as SPA-Bench, macOSWorld and MMBench-GUI, with each benchmark's dataset, environment type, evaluators and venue. It reprints ScreenSpot-Pro and OSWorld leaderboard results and GUI-Odyssey results collected from earlier papers, and names explainability, generalization, security, user-centric tasks and on-device deployment as open challenges. Crossref and the preprint state a CC BY 4.0 license.

name: rabbit r1
summary: Pocket voice-and-touch AI device that serves as a physical channel into rabbit OS3, whose DLAM capability can drive applications on a computer the user connects, with permission.
notes: rabbit inc. lists r1 at $199 USD with no subscription. The r1 page and user guide place computer use in OS3: OS3 works on computers where the rabbit agent is installed, through their terminal, and DLAM, which the guide calls rabbit's computer-use capability, drives an application's screen with the user's permission. The updates log dates a DLAM early-access preview for desktop control via r1 on Windows and Mac to 29 January 2026, BYOK support for DLAM with Anthropic and OpenAI keys to rabbitOS 2.3 (10 July 2026), and OS3 general availability to 22 September 2026. Earlier r1 releases shipped LAM playground, a web agent acting through a webdriver from visual and structured input (1 October 2024), and teach mode, which learned website tasks from demonstrations (21 November 2024); the current user guide describes neither.
read_basis: Read the r1 product page, the r1 user guide (last updated 09/22/2026) and the updates changelog, plus the rabbit OS3 home page. No device purchase, account setup or DLAM run.

name: Kura
summary: Enterprise browser-agent builder whose Recursion agent runs plain-language steps on the live page and saves them as workflow blocks (actions, navigation, extraction, checks) with cached selectors, deployable as APIs.
notes: The homepage says Kura is backed by Y Combinator and lists client-side encryption, stealth browsers, proxy management, credential handling and audit trails. The documentation says the Recursion agent executes each plain-language instruction on the web page in real time and adds the matching blocks to a workflow; Action blocks click, type, press keys and refresh, go back or open, close and switch tabs, alongside navigation, extraction, checkpoint (natural-language assertion), for-loop and conditional blocks. Action and navigation blocks cache the elements or URLs they used and fall back to full reasoning when a cached step fails. A deployed agent gets synchronous and asynchronous API endpoints. The benchmarks page reports 87.0% on 602 of WebVoyager's 643 tasks (41 removed as impossible, booking, login or print tasks) and 90% against 56% for Anthropic's computer-use demo on 50 sampled tasks, for a hierarchical agent of planners, an executor and critics that runs mainly on GPT-4o; these figures are publisher-reported.

name: Retriever AI (rtrvr.ai)
summary: Browser agent from Retriever AI that runs in a Chrome extension on the user's signed-in sessions or in cloud browsers, reading page structure to click, type and fill forms; also callable through an API and MCP.
notes: Retriever AI describes its engine as DOM-native: a planner directs sub-agents for clicks, typing and navigation, DOM extraction, pagination and files, and the same agent runs in the Chrome extension, in Cloud headless browsers (logins carried over by Cookie Sync) and through the API. Free Mode includes supported models and cloud browser time with sponsored cards and a daily allowance; users can bring their own model keys, and schedules, triggers, Cookie Sync and API or MCP control of the user's own Chrome require a paid plan. Recordings capture DOM interactions and the page's own network calls in place of screen recordings, and can be turned into replays or into subroutines that call a site's endpoints directly. An experimental Jev option lets a separate model choose browser actions while the selected model plans. The company also offers Rover, an agent that site owners embed for their visitors, and sells browser-agent trajectories and replica business apps for evaluation. The homepage's Web Bench ranking is a publisher claim.
read_basis: Read the homepage, llms.txt, the Web Agent and Recordings & Grounding docs (markdown), and searched the full docs corpus (llms-full.txt) for the page-observation and action mechanism. No account, extension install or task run.

name: UiPath ScreenPlay
summary: UiPath Studio activity whose Screen Agent turns natural-language task descriptions into self-driving UI automations on Windows, Linux and macOS, using a planner, a pixel grounder, DOM extraction and selectable LLMs.
notes: UiPath describes Screen Agent as the agentic framework behind the ScreenPlay activity in UiPath Studio and Studio Web: a planner turns intent into high-level action sequences, and a targeter that combines a grounder with UiPath's AI Computer Vision resolves pixel coordinates before acting; ScreenPlay adds AI-based DOM extraction. The installation guide offers out-of-the-box Screen Agent variants with Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1 mini, GPT-5 and GPT-5 mini, as well as OpenAI Operator and Anthropic computer use, or bring-your-own-model connections to Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex or an OpenAI V1-compatible provider. The product page says credentials are managed through UiPath Orchestrator and that ScreenPlay resists prompt-injection attacks. UiPath's January 2026 press release and blog report a 67.1% OSWorld-Verified score for the Claude Opus 4.5 variant, then ranked first, and the blog says UiPath also evaluates Screen Agent on its UI-CUBE benchmark; these are publisher statements.

name: Selenium
summary: Browser automation project implementing W3C WebDriver, with Java, Python, Ruby, .NET and JavaScript bindings, Selenium Grid for spreading sessions across machines, and the Rust-based Selenium Manager for driver setup.
notes: The repository README addresses contributors and points users to the documentation on selenium.dev, the project website. The inspected tree holds the WebDriver bindings (java, py, rb, dotnet, javascript), the Java Grid server, the Internet Explorer driver (cpp/iedriver) and Selenium Manager (rust), a command-line tool that locates or downloads browsers and drivers. Selenium IDE, the record-and-playback tool also presented on selenium.dev, lives in the separate SeleniumHQ/selenium-ide repository. Agents use Selenium as an execution layer for browser actions; it contains no agent or model of its own.

details.availability: Published source and language packages; no release was installed or run

read_basis: Read the complete README, rust/README.md at commit 0839e44, the recursive tree at that commit, the root LICENSE, the GitHub repository metadata (id 7613257, not a fork, Apache-2.0) and the selenium.dev home page. No build or test run.

name: Predicate Systems (formerly SentienceAPI)
summary: Runtime trust layer for browser agents: a sidecar checks each action against local policy before it runs, and SDKs turn pages into compact ranked element snapshots and verify outcomes with DOM assertions.
notes: Predicate Systems Inc. was formerly SentienceAPI; www.sentienceapi.com redirects to this site. It has three parts. Predicate Authority is a Rust sidecar that evaluates local YAML policies and issues signed mandates before an action executes. Predicate Runtime, with Python and TypeScript SDKs, collects element geometry through a browser extension, gives the model a structured snapshot of element IDs, roles, text, importance scores and boxes (about 0.6-1.2k tokens per step by the publisher's estimate), executes the chosen action and runs assertions such as url_contains or exists; it runs standalone with Playwright or under browser-use, and an optional Gateway reranks elements with ONNX models. predicate-secure wraps frameworks such as browser-use, Playwright and LangChain with both checks. The documentation also covers Predicate Studio traces and Predicate Vault. New accounts start with 100 free credits.
read_basis: Read the home page, How It Works and the SDK overview documentation, followed the www.sentienceapi.com redirect chain, and checked the PredicateSystems GitHub organization metadata. No account, SDK install or agent run.

name: Yutori
summary: Yutori's web-agent platform: the Navigator computer-use model API (n1.5 for browsers, n2 for full desktops), task APIs for browsing, research and Scout web monitoring, and the Delegate personal agent.
notes: Yutori was founded by Abhishek Das, Devi Parikh and Dhruv Batra and announced its seed round in March 2025. Navigator models are called through an OpenAI Chat Completions-compatible endpoint: the caller sends a screenshot and a task, the model returns actions as tool calls, and the caller executes them and sends a fresh screenshot in an agent loop. n1.5 drives browsers in a normalized 1000x1000 coordinate space with a core set of 18 coordinate-based tools or an expanded set that adds element extraction, find, set_element_value and JavaScript execution, and can return JSON matching a caller schema. n2 operates a full desktop through batched GUI actions plus bash and file tools; the SDK ships local Docker and Daytona examples, and Yutori MCP runs it on the visible macOS desktop, sending screen contents to Yutori. A Python SDK wraps the APIs, a CLI runs research, browsing and Scout tasks, and an MCP server with workflow skills exposes these tasks and computer use to coding agents. Scouts monitor the web on a schedule, and Delegate is a consumer agent meant to complete handed-off tasks independently. Yutori also publishes a computer-use leaderboards page compiling reported results for six benchmarks. The publisher describes its Online-Mind2Web figure as independently verified and its Navi-Bench v2 and Westworld figures as its own evaluations.

name: SMAN-Bench
summary: Evaluation code for SMAN-Bench (Mobile-Bench-v2): AppAgent and Mobile-Agent-v2 runners replay recorded Android pages for single-path, multi-path, noisy and ambiguous tasks, scored by step and task success.
notes: SMAN-Bench is the title of the ICLR 2026 edition of the Mobile-Bench-v2 paper; that edition's proceedings PDF gives this repository as its code and data location, and the README's dataset badge links the Hugging Face release xwk123/MobileBench-v2, which holds the task data. The repository itself has code only, no task files. AppAgent runners draw numbered boxes for clickable and scrollable elements, taken from each recorded page's XML, onto the screenshot; Mobile-Agent-v2 runners (memory unit on, reflection off by default) receive the centre coordinates of the same elements. Single-path and ambiguous runs step through the ground-truth page sequence whatever the agent chooses; multi-path runs move through the recorded page graph according to the agent's actions (default limit 20 rounds) and succeed on reaching the goal page. Ambiguous runs prompt with the task's vague instruction and per-step instructions, or with the complete instruction. eval.py has scorers for single-path, multi-path and noisy runs, printing task success rate, action accuracy and action-type accuracy; the noisy scorer checks the ground-truth click or swipe coordinates against the predicted element's bounds and typed text by character-level F1 above 0.5. Model endpoints are set in config/config.yaml. The README shows an MIT badge, but the tree at the reviewed commit has no LICENSE file. Not a fork, not archived; no release.

details.availability: Public evaluation code (agent runners, scorer and model config); task data is released separately on Hugging Face; no release or tag.

observations: recorded Android screenshots with element boxes drawn from the page XML
actions: scroll a labelled element in a direction
benchmark_protocol.evaluation: Predicted actions are mapped to the recorded action IDs of each page. Single-path runs are scored step by step against the ground-truth path (action accuracy, action-type accuracy, success only when every step matches); multi-path runs succeed when the agent's actions reach the goal page in the recorded page graph; noisy runs check ground-truth click and swipe coordinates against the predicted element's bounds and typed text by character-level F1.
benchmark_protocol.notes: The task files and counts belong to the Hugging Face data release; this repository contains the code. Scoring rules are taken from eval.py at the reviewed commit, which has no separate scorer for the ambiguous split.

code.reason: The README shows an MIT badge linking a LICENSE file, but the complete tree at the reviewed commit has no license file, so no grant is established.

name: LongHorizonUI
summary: Code for the LongHorizonUI Android agent: OCR plus OmniParser icon detection yields numbered element boxes for an LLM, and failed taps fall back from element index to relative and absolute points with rollback.
notes: Code release of the ICLR 2026 paper "LongHorizonUI: A Unified Framework for Robust long-horizon Task Automation of GUI Agent" (the repository description says ICLR2026; the README cites it with anonymous authors and no link). Each screenshot passes through RapidOCR, the OmniParser v2 YOLO icon detector (downloaded from microsoft/OmniParser-v2.0 on first use) and template matching when an icon template directory is set; the merged elements are drawn as numbered boxes, and that annotated screenshot with a step prompt is what the Gemini, Azure OpenAI or OpenAI model receives. Actions are click, long press, swipe, drag, text input and key press. With the fallback cascade on (the default), an element-index target that fails is retried as a relative point inside the box and then as absolute coordinates with jitter; a progress monitor can roll back to the last committed snapshot, at most three times per task. The README documents only the offline mode, which replays a task's recorded screenshot sequence with either the task description or step-by-step instructions. run.py also has a live subcommand that lists USB-connected devices, but at the reviewed commit AndroidContext never opens a device connection (its context stays None), so device actions return without acting. The repository also has a Gradio app, agents that turn recorded taps and swipes into step descriptions, a scrcpy-based Android recording tool, step-level evaluation scripts and the project page source. The LongGUIBench dataset is not released (the README link is a placeholder), the requirements.txt the README installs from is not in the tree, and the README's Apache-2.0 badge and LICENSE link are not backed by a license file. Not a fork, not archived; no release.

details.availability: Public source for the agent, demo app, recorder and evaluation scripts; the LongGUIBench dataset and a requirements file remain outside the repository, with no release published.

code.reason: The README shows an Apache-2.0 badge and links a LICENSE file, but the complete tree at the reviewed commit has no license file, so no grant is established.

name: Computer Agent Arena
summary: Crowdsourced arena where users pit two computer-use agents against each other on Ubuntu or Windows VMs; the repository holds the voting frontend, setup presets and 2,010 verified battle sessions.
notes: Platform code from the xlang-ai organization; the repository description and README name ICLR 2026. At the reviewed commit (the second of two) the tree holds the React/TypeScript frontend (dual-agent chat and evaluation panels, a bundled noVNC desktop viewer, trajectory player, ranking and Prolific pages), quick-setup presets for Chrome, LibreOffice and other apps, setup notes for OSWorld's in-VM server and for AWS, VMware and VirtualBox providers, backend/requirements.txt and backend/scripts/sessions_clean_filtered.csv. Although the README describes the full stack, the tree has no Python source: there is no backend/main.py, the server notes refer to main.py and pyxcursor.py files that are absent, and backend/agents is a git submodule pointing to xlang-ai/computer-agent-arena-hub, which the GitHub API did not return at review (404). The CSV has 2,010 verified two-agent sessions started between 2025-02-13 and 2025-05-15 (1,070 Windows, 940 Ubuntu; 653 distinct user IDs) with user-written task instructions, each agent's model and method, per-step feedback and the battle result (751 and 644 wins for the first and second agent, 615 ties). Agents in it are Claude 3.5 and 3.7 Sonnet computer use, OpenAI computer-use-preview, UI-TARS-1.5, a Qwen2.5-VL-72B agent, and GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, o3, o4-mini and Gemini models through a base agent. The frontend evaluation form asks for each agent's correctness (correct, partially correct, wrong) and a pairwise preference (A better, tie, B better, tie with both bad). The README shows an MIT badge and links a LICENSE file, but the tree has no root license file; its only license texts are those of the bundled noVNC viewer. Not a fork, not archived; no release.

details.availability: Frontend source, setup presets and notes, and a CSV of verified battle sessions; backend server and agent hub source remain outside this repository, with no release published.

focus: human pairwise preference between computer-use agents
observations: live Ubuntu or Windows virtual machine desktop shown to the user through VNC
benchmark_protocol.evaluation: After two agents attempt the same user task on separate virtual machines, the user rates each agent's correctness (correct, partially correct, wrong) and states a pairwise preference (A better, tie, B better, or tie with both bad); per-step feedback is also recorded. The README says the votes feed an ELO leaderboard; the aggregation backend remains outside this repository.
benchmark_protocol.notes: Counts are rows of the released CSV, computed with Python's csv module; each row is one session with two agents and a distinct session ID. Agent observations and actions are defined by the agent implementations in the unreleased hub.

code.reason: The README shows an MIT badge and links a LICENSE file, but the complete tree at the reviewed commit has no root license file; its only license texts belong to the bundled noVNC viewer under frontend/public/noVNC, so no grant is established for the repository's own code.

name: OSReward
summary: Evaluator and collection code for OSReward, which tests VLM judges' SUCCESS/FAIL verdicts on human-labelled computer-use trajectories, plus web, Windows, Android and Ubuntu trajectory pipelines.
notes: Code for the OSReward paper; the trajectories themselves are released separately on Hugging Face as OS-Copilot/OSReward (the README reports 1,019 Full and 284 Hard trajectories with screenshots and human verdicts), alongside the gated OS-Shepherd-100K corpus and OS-Shepherd checkpoints. eval_pipeline/run_judge.py downloads the Full or Hard Parquet split (or reads local traces), sends a judge the full thought and action history and, by default, the last five screenshots with red markers at normalized action points, at temperature 0, through an OpenAI-compatible or native Anthropic API, and parses one 'Judge: SUCCESS' or 'Judge: FAIL' verdict per trajectory. It reports accuracy, balanced accuracy, SUCCESS and FAIL recall and coverage; missing, failed and unparseable outputs count as incorrect. Its subset option offers full, hard and custom, with no OSReward-Multi option, although the README roadmap lists Multi under the evaluation harness. trajectory_collection/ holds the collection pipelines: webtrail for live and self-hosted websites, a Windows Agent Arena based Windows 11 VM pipeline, an AndroidWorld based emulator pipeline, and an OSWorld based Ubuntu pipeline with a screenshot-only tool-call agent (the root README calls Ubuntu 'on the way' and the collection README calls it a placeholder, but its code is in the tree), plus export_judged_sft.py for judge-SFT bundles. benchmarking_analysis/ scores judges against the ground-truth labels of OSWorld, WindowsAgentArena, WebArena and AndroidWorld rollouts, with small samples under data/raw. The OS-Shepherd-100K construction pipeline and the OS-Shepherd training and inference code are listed as pending release. There is no root LICENSE; the bundled Windows and Android pipelines carry Microsoft's MIT and the Apache-2.0 license texts. Not a fork, not archived; no release.

details.availability: Public evaluator, collection pipelines and judge analysis; benchmark data, corpus and checkpoints are on Hugging Face; corpus construction and reward-model training code remain pending release, with no release or tag for this repository.

focus: reliability of VLM judges and reward models on computer-use trajectories
observations: last five screenshots with red action-point markers (default)
actions: one SUCCESS or FAIL verdict per trajectory
benchmark_protocol.evaluation: Verdicts are compared with human gold labels; the evaluator reports accuracy, balanced accuracy, SUCCESS recall, FAIL recall and coverage, counting missing, API-error and unparseable outputs as incorrect.

counts.population: OSReward Full split on Hugging Face
